errors.location: Section III, paragraph immediately after Eq. (4)
errors.description: The claimed T-fold SINR improvement does not follow from a unitary F_b. A unitary matrix has unit-norm rows, so matched filtering with f_{b,n}† does not collect T times the signal energy; that gain would require orthogonal rows with squared norm T or a different stated energy normalization.
errors.evidence: “If the matrix F_b is unitary, the data symbols x_{b,n} can be recovered without crosstalk by the matched filters f_{b,n}† that provide the T-fold improvement of SINR.”

errors.location: Eq. (3) and the first numerical example in Section IV
errors.description: T is used as a matrix dimension in F_b ∈ C^{T×T} and as the number of columns in T_b, but the first numerical example sets T = 18.375. A fractional value cannot be a matrix dimension, so this example is not represented by the stated discrete matrix model.
errors.evidence: “For some matrix F_b ∈ C^{T × T} ... allow for a more general N × T transmit matrix” (Eq. 3); later, “we set T = 18.375.”

errors.location: Final summary claim about spatial multiplexing and peak data rate
errors.description: The unqualified claim that peak data rate grows linearly with SNR conflates adding spatial streams with rate scaling in SNR. With a finite number of spatial dimensions, spatial multiplexing adds parallel channels, while each channel's rate follows a logarithmic dependence on SNR as in Eq. (9); the linear approximation in Eq. (10) is limited to low SNR and does not establish linear peak-rate growth.
errors.evidence: The summary says, “Peak data rate can be made to grow linearly with SNR by means of spatial multiplexing,” while Eq. (9) gives “R = log_2(1 + SNR)” and Eq. (10) labels its linear form as an approximation for SNR ≪ 1.
